newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: More S.African mines turn marginal as gold slumps.
newsitem.headline: More S.African mines turn marginal as gold slumps.

text.p: Bullion's tumble to 3-1/4 year lows has increased the number of marginal mines operating in South Africa and dampened the outlook for gold shares this year, industry analysts said on Tuesday.
But although the gold price was seen sliding further, most mines were not expected to trim production in 1997 as a weak rand was cushioning them from the full effects of the slump in dollar terms.

Roger Baxter, the senior economist at the Chamber of Mines, said marginal mines, those with a working profit to working revenue ratio of less than seven percent, had risen to nine from six during the third quarter.
The chamber's 23 gold mining members produce more than 95 percent of South Africa's gold.
Gold mining quarterly results for the fourth quarter are due to be released from next week.
"I don't foresee it in the short term having any impact on production," Baxter told Reuters.
"I foresee production actually stabilising at roughly the 500 tonne level (for 1997)."

The mining industry is expected to have produced only 490-495 tonnes of gold in 1996 -- its lowest output since 1956 and some six percent down on 1995's 522.4 tonnes. Final year figures are expected to be released at the start of February.

Bullion sank to a fresh low in London on Tuesday fixing at $357.65 per ounce, its weakest level since October 6, 1993. Gold has fallen more than $10 in the first week of 1997 under selling pressure from speculators and U.S.-based investment funds.

But analysts said only the most marginal of mines were likely to reduce output at the current gold price which is still around the average for 1996, at 1,670 rand an ounce, although well down on the peak of over 1,800 rand hit last October.
"It is still profitable. If productivity improvements come through the outlook could be fairly positive," said Dean Cunningham, a gold analyst at Investec Fergusson.
He said he expected better productivity from mines in the Gengold stable, notably Beatrix Mines Ltd, and across-the-board at mines in the Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd group.
Baxter said some of the country's highest cost producers were also protected from weak bullion by hedging programmes.
"The industry is also really focusing on investing in human capital, reorganising work practices, using the time available for mining and in some cases restructuring mining operations," Baxter said.
But other analysts warned of problems for the industry if the gold price experienced further sharp falls.

"I don't think the gold price drop is over yet. I think gold could go to $350 and then $330...If it gets to those levels we should look at the whole thing again," said Nick Goodwin, gold analyst at Fedsure Asset Management.

South African gold shares have borne the brunt of bullion's slide, with the all gold 100 percent index at its lowest level in a year and down almost seven percent since the start of 1997. The index gained 12.1 percent in value over the whole of 1996.
Analysts were divided on whether shares offered buying potential.

"Even at these levels I see buying opportunities coming through for institutions and gold traders...We have gone down to these levels before and all of a sudden this has been the level at which people come in and buy," Cunningham said.
But Goodwin, warning of a possible fall in the gold index to below the 1,000 level this year from 1,402.9 at 1130 GMT on Tuesday, said: "I would just avoid it."
-- Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
